newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Large bond issues highlight Latin debt burden.
newsitem.headline: Large bond issues highlight Latin debt burden.

text.p: Argentina and Mexico raced to be first with large global bond issues early in 1997, reminding investors of the challenges Latin American countries face in dealing with their debt burdens.

This month, Argentina raised $2.0 billion through a 20-year global bond issue while Mexico raised $1.0 billion with a 10-year global bond. High international liquidity levels allowed both nations to lock in cheap rates.
But timing of the issues underlined worries about a likely rise in U.S. rates and upcoming votes in the two countries.

With this month's $2.0 billion issue, Argentina has already covered almost half the $8.5 billion in foreign debt it plans to issue this year. In December, it sold $2.0 billion worth of bonds covering 1997 needs. It plans to issue a further $1.0 billion before the end of March.
Argentine officials have cited investor concerns as one factor behind their move to issue such a large portion of the nation's debt early in the year.
"There are worries overseas about Argentina's ability to obtain financing," said Argentina's Undersecretary of Finance Miguel Kiguel.
Argentina will be the area's largest foreign issuer in 1997. Mexico projects total new issuance of $4.41 billion, and analysts forecast Brazil may match the $1.5 billion it placed last year.

Newer issuers such as Ecuador may attract more attention this year as investors seek to repeat their hefty 1996 returns. Ecuador's government plans to launch its first-ever Eurobond this year, with Chase Manhattan expected to lead.
Experts said Ecuador's success in credit markets hinges on the success of an ambitious economic program launched by Ecuador's President Abdala Bucaram.
"If Ecuador is able to carry out its reforms, for sure our bonds will deliver the strongest returns" in the region this year, Jose Mantilla, Ecuador's former Treasury Undersecretary, told Reuters.
The program, which faces stiff opposition, includes cost-cutting, privatizations and the introduction of "convertibility," fixing the value of the sucre to the dollar.

Social tensions mounted in Ecuador this month after steep public tariff hikes led to questions about the currency convertability plan. Ecuador's financial markets were bracing last week for a possible run on the dollar and jump in interest rates if currency reforms did not win broad support.

While much of Latin America continues to rely on overseas financing amid low domestic savings rates and shallow capital markets, Brazil is one big debtor that is taking steps in the other direction. Still, analysts said Brazil faces its own difficulties: its stock of domestic debt is overwhelmingly denominated in very short maturities.

Maturities on Brazil's weekly central bank bond issues are just 56 days and the average maturity on National Treasury paper is about four months. The two institutions roll over more than $120 billion in domestic debt every four months.
Analysts said Brazil's biggest challenge is to lengthen those maturities to reduce interest costs.

In October, Brazil's net public debt was $250 billion, of which only $33 billion was external debt, compared with Argentina at the other extreme with $57 billion worth of bonds denominated in foreign currencies and $6.8 billion in pesos.
On the bright side, many Latin nations expect debt as a percentage of gross domestic product to fall or stabilize this year as the recovery that started in 1996 consolidates.

Mexico President Ernesto Zedillo has pointed out that Mexico has the lowest debt-to-GDP ratio of any Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development member, and Argentine President Carlos Menem can cite debt levels well below the Maastricht Treaty criteria on Europe's single currency plan.

Mexico's total external debt is seen falling to 45.1 percent of GDP this year from 48.3 percent in 1996 according to Santander Investments. Venezuela's is anticipated to fall to 48 percent from 50 percent.

Gustavo Franco, the international affairs director of Brazil's central bank, has said his country's net public sector debt is likely to stabilize at about 35 percent of GDP at the end of this year from 34.2 percent in October.
Argentina's Kiguel stressed, "Debt continues to be a problem in Latin America but we no longer have high current account deficits nor fiscal imbalances like in the 1980s."
((--Buenos Aires Newsroom, 541 318-0668))
